abstract: Salamanders are an enduring and historically significant group that helped originate multiple scientific fields of study, including regeneration, cytogenetics, experimental embryology, cloning, evolutionary developmental biology and evolution of extreme genome size. We generated a high-quality, single haplotype assembly for the 32 Gb axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) genome using an F1 hybrid between axolotl and a divergent relative the tiger salamander (A. tigrinum). Using multi-genome alignments to other salamanders that meet VGP metrics, we leveraged strong conservation of karyotypic structure to identify >523,000 highly conserved non-coding elements within massively expanded intronic and intergenic regions, the vast majority of which are unique to the salamander lineage. Orthogonal measures of chromatin state and enhancer activity confirmed that many conserved elements correspond to cis-regulatory sequences and identified several thousand that are utilized during regeneration. The conserved elements identified here will enable robust functional genomic analyses of tissue regeneration and other traits that uniquely empower salamander models in biological research.
